content: Ovarian cancer is the sixth most common cancer affecting women. Primary surgery for ovarian cancer serves not only to confirm the diagnosis and determine the stage of the disease but also to achieve optimal cytoreduction. Cytoreduction refers to the surgical removal of as much of the tumor as possible, as the amount of residual tumor left after surgery is one of the most critical prognostic factors for survival in women with epithelial ovarian cancer. The definition of an optimal surgical outcome in cytoreductive surgery remains a topic of debate among gynecologic oncologists. According to the Gynaecologic Oncology Group (GOG), optimal cytoreduction is defined as leaving behind residual tumor nodules that are 1 cm or less in maximum diameter, with the ideal outcome being complete cytoreduction, where no visible tumor remains (microscopic disease). Although smaller residual tumor size after surgery has been shown to correlate with better outcomes in advanced ovarian cancer, it is unclear whether the improved survival is directly attributable to the surgical procedure itself or to other factors related to the patient or the disease. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of optimal primary cytoreductive surgery in women with surgically staged advanced epithelial ovarian cancer (stages III and IV). Additionally, the review aimed to assess the impact of varying residual tumor sizes, ranging from zero to 2 cm, on overall survival (OS). To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to August 2010. The search also included clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of relevant studies, and consultations with experts in the field. The inclusion criteria for the review were retrospective data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective and retrospective observational studies. These studies had to include a multivariate analysis of at least 100 adult women with surgically staged advanced epithelial ovarian cancer who underwent primary cytoreductive surgery followed by adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy. Only studies that defined optimal cytoreduction as leaving residual tumors with a maximum diameter of up to 2 cm were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Where possible, the data were synthesized into a meta-analysis. No RCTs or prospective non-RCTs were identified that specifically evaluated the effectiveness of primary cytoreductive surgery in advanced ovarian cancer. However, 11 retrospective studies met the inclusion criteria and included multivariate analyses. These studies demonstrated the prognostic importance of achieving complete cytoreduction, where no visible residual disease remains. Women with microscopic residual disease had significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) compared to those with visible residual disease. Although not all studies reported PFS, the available data were sufficient to draw firm conclusions. When comparing suboptimal cytoreduction (residual disease > 1 cm) to optimal cytoreduction (residual disease < 1 cm), survival outcomes were better in the group with smaller residual disease, although the differences were less pronounced. When comparing residual disease of > 2 cm to < 2 cm, there was no significant difference in OS and only a borderline difference in PFS (hazard ratio [HR] 1.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.82 to 3.31 for OS; HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.61, P = 0.05 for PFS). The retrospective nature of the included studies introduced a high risk of bias. Despite statistical adjustments for important prognostic factors, selection bias likely influenced the results. Additionally, none of the studies adequately reported adverse events, quality of life (QoL), or cost-effectiveness by treatment arm. The authors concluded that during primary surgery for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, every effort should be made to achieve complete cytoreduction. If complete cytoreduction is not possible, the surgical goal should be to achieve optimal cytoreduction, defined as residual disease < 1 cm. Given the high risk of bias in the current evidence, randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether improved survival is due to the surgical intervention itself or to patientand disease-related factors. The findings of this review suggest that women with residual disease < 1 cm have better outcomes than those with residual disease > 1 cm. This observation should encourage the surgical community to retain the category of optimal cytoreduction for residual disease < 1 cm and consider redefining it as near-optimal cytoreduction. The term suboptimal cytoreduction could then be reserved for cases where residual disease exceeds 1 cm. This reclassification would replace the current terminology of complete/optimal/suboptimal with optimal/near-optimal/suboptimal cytoreduction.
